agent_trace.summary: On MRI, the signal appearance of intracranial hemorrhage changes predictably over time as hemoglobin breaks down. A hypointense hemorrhage typically reflects blood products containing deoxyhemoglobin or hemosiderin, which usually suggests a subacute-to-chronic stage or prior/older bleed depending on the sequence used.

key_facts: Hemorrhage signal on MRI evolves with time because hemoglobin degradation products have different magnetic properties.
Hypointensity on T2*/GRE or susceptibility-sensitive sequences often indicates blood products such as deoxyhemoglobin or hemosiderin.
Acute hemorrhage is more often associated with oxyhemoglobin early, then deoxyhemoglobin, while chronic blood products can remain hypointense due to hemosiderin.
The exact stage depends on the MRI sequence and the age of the bleed; hypointensity generally implies older blood than a bright, methemoglobin-rich subacute bleed.
In the brain, hemorrhage may be seen in the parenchyma, ventricles, or extra-axial spaces, with associated mass effect or edema depending on severity.
